name: Medical Devices Regulation
impact_assessment: joint impact assessment SWD(2012) 273 (executive summary SWD(2012) 274)
evidence_rating: moderate: monitoring surveys for the Commission and national shortage data that measure device withdrawals and certification times, plus the Commission's targeted evaluation; no causal study of effects on safety or innovation
summary: The Regulation has applied since May 2021, with transition periods extended several times. The Commission's 2025 targeted evaluation found safety and transparency improving but compliance costs high and often disproportionate. In surveys for the Commission's monitoring study, 48% of responding manufacturers had withdrawn some devices from the EU since 2021, most because revenue did not justify recertification, and notified bodies report that most new certificates take more than a year. The only before-and-after test found, for AI imaging devices, shows no change in the gap between EU and US approval. A targeted revision proposed in December 2025 is estimated to save about EUR 3.3 billion a year.

indicators.objective: No monitoring indicators set in the proposal; assessed through the Commission's reports listed below
High level of safety while supporting innovation
indicators.indicator: Availability of devices; certification times and costs
indicators.evidence: 2025: safety and transparency benefits materialising; longer and costlier market access; decrease in availability of some devices.

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), Targeted evaluation of Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices, SWD(2025) 1051
literature.title: Targeted evaluation of Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices
literature.outcomes: safety; compliance costs; device availability; innovation
literature.headline: Benefits for patients materialising through stronger safety, performance and transparency, but at high and often disproportionate cost; implementation delays, longer and costlier market access, limited notified-body capacity; decrease in availability of some, particularly innovative and niche, devices
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's own evaluation found the stricter rules make devices safer and more transparent, but are costly and slow enough that some devices, especially new and niche ones, have left or not reached the EU market.
literature.quality: Commission self-assessment; data on costs limited

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), Cost-savings accompanying the proposal amending Regulations (EU) 2017/745 and 2017/746, SWD(2025) 1050
literature.title: Cost-savings accompanying the proposal amending Regulations (EU) 2017/745 and 2017/746
literature.headline: Simplification measures in the December 2025 proposal estimated to save around EUR 3.3 billion a year (EUR 0.9 billion adjustment and EUR 2.4 billion administrative costs)
literature.summary_plain: For its proposed simplification, the Commission estimates savings for industry of about EUR 3.3 billion a year.

literature.citation: Austrian National Public Health Institute (GÖG); Areté; Civic Consulting (2026), Study supporting the monitoring of availability of medical devices on the EU market - study overview and survey results of the 3rd economic operator survey (data status 31 October 2025), Report for European Commission DG SANTE / HaDEA (EU4Health, SC 2021 P3 03)
literature.authors: Austrian National Public Health Institute (GÖG); Areté; Civic Consulting
literature.title: Study supporting the monitoring of availability of medical devices on the EU market - study overview and survey results of the 3rd economic operator survey (data status 31 October 2025)
literature.venue: Report for European Commission DG SANTE / HaDEA (EU4Health, SC 2021 P3 03)
literature.method: repeated online surveys of manufacturers and authorised representatives (3rd wave n=213; 152 MD manufacturers answered discontinuation question)
literature.outcomes: discontinuation of devices from the EU market; reasons; orphan/niche devices; certification status
literature.headline: 48% of responding MD manufacturers (73/152) had stopped producing, marketing or supplying some devices on the EU market since 2021. 63% of these named 'product revenue does not justify cost to reapprove device under the MDR' as a main reason, and 7% (5/73) said orphan or niche devices were affected.
literature.summary_plain: In the Commission's own monitoring survey, about half of responding device makers had pulled at least some products from the EU, mostly because re-certifying them under the MDR cost more than they earned.
literature.quality: descriptive; self-selected survey sample (n=152 for this item); official

literature.citation: Austrian National Public Health Institute (GÖG); Areté; Civic Consulting (2025), Study supporting the monitoring of availability of medical devices on the EU market - health service provider survey results (incl. Zorg Inkoop Netwerk Nederland shortage data), Report for European Commission DG SANTE / HaDEA
literature.authors: Austrian National Public Health Institute (GÖG); Areté; Civic Consulting
literature.title: Study supporting the monitoring of availability of medical devices on the EU market - health service provider survey results (incl. Zorg Inkoop Netwerk Nederland shortage data)
literature.venue: Report for European Commission DG SANTE / HaDEA
literature.method: survey of health service providers (n=55) plus Dutch national shortage-reporting data (ZINN, 3 Jul 2023-31 Mar 2025)
literature.outcomes: supply problems; reported potential shortages and their causes; availability of alternatives
literature.headline: 45% of health service providers reported MDR-related supply problems in the previous six months. In Dutch shortage reports (2,634 devices, Jul 2023-Mar 2025), 36.1% were 'product will not be MDR certified' and 13.1% 'MDR certificate not in time'. A one-to-one alternative existed in 42.9% of cases and none in 1.5%.
literature.summary_plain: Hospitals report real shortages linked to the MDR, and in Dutch data about half of flagged device shortages trace back to MDR certification, although most had a substitute.
literature.quality: descriptive; small survey; national registry data with supplier-reported reasons

literature.citation: EY for European Commission, DG SANTE (2025), Study on regulatory governance and innovation in the field of medical devices - Final report, Publications Office of the EU (ISBN 978-92-68-34983-0)
literature.authors: EY for European Commission, DG SANTE
literature.title: Study on regulatory governance and innovation in the field of medical devices - Final report
literature.method: literature/secondary data review, online survey (n=470), 41 interviews, workshops, international benchmarking
literature.outcomes: portfolio reductions; market exits; innovation; governance effectiveness
literature.headline: 57% of survey respondents had reduced their device portfolios and 24% had stopped producing devices for the EU market, with portfolio cuts reported by 69% of large firms vs 13% of SMEs. Only 11% expected the MDR/IVDR to significantly support innovation over the next 5-10 years, while 34% said it would not.
literature.summary_plain: A Commission-funded study finds many firms have narrowed what they sell in the EU and few think the new rules help innovation.
literature.quality: descriptive; stakeholder survey and interviews; no counterfactual
literature.verified: publisher page abstract read; survey figures from RAPS news summary (19 Jan 2026), not checked against the PDF

literature.citation: Kadakia, K.T.; Lalani, C.; Kramer, D.B.; Orui, H.; Yeh, R.W. (2024), Market of First Launch for High-Risk Therapeutic Medical Devices, JAMA Network Open 7(12):e2449298
literature.authors: Kadakia, K.T.; Lalani, C.; Kramer, D.B.; Orui, H.; Yeh, R.W.
literature.title: Market of First Launch for High-Risk Therapeutic Medical Devices
literature.method: cross-sectional analysis of FDA PMA class III therapeutic devices 2013-2023 and their first-launch market
literature.outcomes: share of US-first vs international-first launches; time lags; recalls
literature.headline: Of 230 devices, 80.0% launched internationally first and 20.0% in the US first, but US-first launches rose from 2 in 2013 to 12 in 2023 (P = .001 for trend). Recalls hit 31.5% of international-first vs 19.6% of US-first devices.
literature.summary_plain: High-risk devices are increasingly launched in the US before Europe, consistent with Europe losing its first-launch role, though the study does not test the MDR directly.
literature.quality: descriptive; does not mention or isolate the MDR; trend only

literature.citation: Siontis, G.; Windecker, D.; Fraser, A.; Caiani, E.G.; Ren, Y. (2026), Regulatory time-lag between CE-marking and FDA approval of artificial intelligence softwares, European Heart Journal 47(Suppl 1) (ESC Congress abstract)
literature.authors: Siontis, G.; Windecker, D.; Fraser, A.; Caiani, E.G.; Ren, Y.
literature.title: Regulatory time-lag between CE-marking and FDA approval of artificial intelligence softwares
literature.method: cross-sectional; Kaplan-Meier time to second approval before vs after MDR (May 2021); Cox regression
literature.outcomes: time between CE-marking and FDA clearance for AI radiology devices
literature.headline: Among 239 AI radiology devices, median time to second approval was 54 months and did not differ before vs after MDR implementation (log-rank p=0.17). CE-first devices waited longer for FDA clearance than FDA-first devices waited for CE (median 17.5 vs 3.5 months).
literature.summary_plain: For AI imaging software, the MDR did not measurably change how long it takes to get approved on both sides of the Atlantic.
literature.period_geography: EU and US, AI radiology devices, pre/post 2021
literature.quality: before-after comparison; conference abstract, not peer-reviewed full paper; CORE-MD (EU Horizon) authors

literature.citation: McDermott, O.; Folan, M.; Stafylas, P.C. (2026), An impact assessment of the European medical device regulations implementation - the current status quo, Expert Review of Medical Devices 23(9):1137-1148
literature.authors: McDermott, O.; Folan, M.; Stafylas, P.C.
literature.title: An impact assessment of the European medical device regulations implementation - the current status quo
literature.method: quantitative survey of medical device enterprises (micro to large)
literature.outcomes: launch location; portfolio rationalisation; regulatory costs
literature.headline: Reports that the MDR/IVDR 'has harmed innovation, leading many manufacturers to seek initial device approval and launch elsewhere'. Firms have removed devices from the market, and costs have risen through notified-body fees, documentation, recertification and staff, so the EU 'is no longer the market of choice for new products'.
literature.summary_plain: Device makers surveyed say the new rules have pushed them to launch first outside Europe and to drop some products.
literature.quality: descriptive; industry self-report survey; sample size not stated in abstract

literature.citation: Kearney, B.; McDermott, O. (2023), The Challenges for Manufacturers of the Increased Clinical Evaluation in the European Medical Device Regulations: A Quantitative Study, Therapeutic Innovation & Regulatory Science 57(4):783-796
literature.title: The Challenges for Manufacturers of the Increased Clinical Evaluation in the European Medical Device Regulations: A Quantitative Study
literature.method: quantitative survey of 68 regulatory/quality experts in device manufacturers
literature.outcomes: clinical evaluation burden; outsourcing; launch strategy; device withdrawals
literature.headline: Over 60% of high-risk device manufacturers outsourced clinical evaluation reports, and 41.7% of the high-risk group launched in another market before CE marking (vs 20% medium-risk). 'Approx. 54% of respondents have or are planning to remove' devices from the EU market.
literature.summary_plain: Firms say the MDR's tougher clinical-evidence rules are costly and are leading some to launch elsewhere first or withdraw products.
literature.quality: descriptive; small convenience survey (n=68); denominators for subgroup percentages unclear

literature.citation: Carl, A.-K.; Hochmann, D. (2023), Impact of the new European medical device regulation: a two-year comparison, Biomedizinische Technik / Biomedical Engineering 69(3):317-326
literature.title: Impact of the new European medical device regulation: a two-year comparison
literature.method: two repeated cross-sectional surveys of orthopaedic-aids firms (pre-application n=146; ~2 years later n=233)
literature.headline: Firms of all sizes in the orthopaedic-aids sector struggled with the MDR, citing documentation workload, cost and unclear requirements. 'Many companies are downsizing their product portfolio', raising the risk of supply shortages.
literature.summary_plain: Makers of orthopaedic aids such as braces and prostheses say the MDR is costly and is making them cut product lines.

literature.citation: Team-NB (European Association of Medical Devices Notified Bodies) (2026), Medical Device Survey 2025 - data from all 41 designated members, Team-NB survey report
literature.authors: Team-NB (European Association of Medical Devices Notified Bodies)
literature.title: Medical Device Survey 2025 - data from all 41 designated members
literature.method: annual survey of 41 member notified bodies (out of 52 designated; c.79% market share)
literature.outcomes: certificates issued; time to certification; certificate withdrawals
literature.headline: By end-2025 members had issued 17,260 MDR/IVDR certificates. For a new MDR certificate, 48% took 13-18 months, 15% took 19-24 months and 7% over 24 months; only 14% took under 6 months.
literature.summary_plain: Notified bodies are now issuing many more certificates, but getting a new device certified under the MDR typically still takes more than a year.
literature.interested_party: notified bodies' trade association (certifiers paid by manufacturers)

literature.citation: MedTech Europe (2025), MedTech Europe IVDR & MDR Survey Results 2024 - Report Highlights, MedTech Europe report
literature.title: MedTech Europe IVDR & MDR Survey Results 2024 - Report Highlights
literature.method: online survey of manufacturers, Apr-May 2024 (138 MD and 73 IVD manufacturers)
literature.outcomes: certification time and cost; first-launch geography; innovation activity
literature.headline: Average MDR certification took 19.5 months for QMS and 21.8 months for technical documentation. Choosing the EU as first-launch market fell from 72% to 39% of large MD firms and from 77% to 58% of MD SMEs (a drop of 33% and 19%). Certification and maintenance costs rose 'up to 100% (or more)' vs the directives.
literature.summary_plain: The industry association's survey says getting devices certified now takes nearly two years and that far fewer firms launch new devices in Europe first.
literature.period_geography: EU, before vs after MDR/IVDR application (recall-based)
literature.quality: descriptive; industry self-report with retrospective before/after recall
literature.interested_party: MedTech Europe (industry trade association lobbying for MDR/IVDR revision)

literature.citation: Bonan, A.; Huynh, S.; Pineau, J.; Sabatier, B.; Martelli, N. (2025), Impact du Règlement Européen sur les dispositifs médicaux sur leur disponibilité : scoping review et analyse sur deux ans du risque pour les patients dans le domaine cardiovasculaire, Annales Pharmaceutiques Françaises 83(3):428-437
literature.authors: Bonan, A.; Huynh, S.; Pineau, J.; Sabatier, B.; Martelli, N.
literature.title: Impact du Règlement Européen sur les dispositifs médicaux sur leur disponibilité : scoping review et analyse sur deux ans du risque pour les patients dans le domaine cardiovasculaire
literature.method: scoping review plus two-year analysis of cardiovascular device unavailability in a French university hospital
literature.outcomes: availability of cardiovascular devices; clinical practice impacts
literature.headline: High-risk cardiovascular devices 'appear to be heavily impacted', and some manufacturers focus on innovative devices 'at the expense of marketing existing product lines'. Unavailability affected patient care and led clinicians to request exceptional national exemptions.
literature.summary_plain: A Paris hospital study finds some heart devices became unavailable under the MDR, forcing doctors to seek special exemptions.

literature.citation: Siontis, G.C.M.; Coles, B.; Häner, J.D.; et al. (CORE-MD Investigators) (2024), Quality and transparency of evidence for implantable cardiovascular medical devices assessed by the CORE-MD consortium, European Heart Journal 45(3):161-177
literature.authors: Siontis, G.C.M.; Coles, B.; Häner, J.D.; et al. (CORE-MD Investigators)
literature.title: Quality and transparency of evidence for implantable cardiovascular medical devices assessed by the CORE-MD consortium
literature.method: systematic review of prospective studies for 71 high-risk cardiovascular devices relative to CE-mark date, 2000-2021
literature.outcomes: quantity and quality of pre- and post-CE clinical evidence
literature.headline: Of 308 prospective studies, 81% were non-randomised. No RCT was published before CE-mark approval for any device, and 89% of non-randomised trials appeared after CE marking. Larger trials became more frequent in 2016-21.
literature.summary_plain: A baseline review shows that, up to 2021, high-risk heart implants reached the EU market with little published high-quality evidence, which is the gap the MDR is meant to close.
literature.quality: systematic review; mostly pre-MDR baseline, not a test of MDR effects

literature.citation: Hulstaert, F.; Pouppez, C.; Primus-de Jong, C.; Harkin, K.; Neyt, M. (2023), Gaps in the evidence underpinning high-risk medical devices in Europe at market entry, and potential solutions, Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases 18:212
literature.authors: Hulstaert, F.; Pouppez, C.; Primus-de Jong, C.; Harkin, K.; Neyt, M.
literature.title: Gaps in the evidence underpinning high-risk medical devices in Europe at market entry, and potential solutions
literature.method: review of 18 Belgian payer (RIZIV-INAMI) assessor reports on novel class IIb-III devices (2018-mid-2019), plus literature and legal review
literature.outcomes: level of clinical evidence at market entry
literature.headline: Only 7 of 18 applications (39%) included an RCT of the novel device, half lacked quality-of-life data and 22% had no data beyond 12 months. The authors conclude the MDR still does not require evidence of clinical effectiveness and cite a first report showing 'no improvement' under the MDR.
literature.summary_plain: Belgian payer files show many high-risk devices still arrive with weak evidence, and the authors argue the MDR has not fixed this.
literature.quality: descriptive; small sample; authors from Belgian HTA agency (KCE)

literature.citation: Dobrzynska, A.; Rejón-Parrilla, J.C.; Epstein, D.M.; Aranda-López, J.; Fraser, A.G.; Blasco-Amaro, J.A. (2025), Survey of Notified Bodies reveals very limited use of conditional certification for high-risk medical devices, Frontiers in Medical Technology 7:1504294
literature.authors: Dobrzynska, A.; Rejón-Parrilla, J.C.; Epstein, D.M.; Aranda-López, J.; Fraser, A.G.; Blasco-Amaro, J.A.
literature.title: Survey of Notified Bodies reveals very limited use of conditional certification for high-risk medical devices
literature.outcomes: use of restrictions/limitations on certificates for class III and IIb implantables
literature.headline: Of 13 notified bodies responding, only 3 had issued certificates with restrictions or limitations. NBs reported difficulty collecting and providing data on conditional certification.
literature.summary_plain: Certifiers rarely use the MDR's option to approve high-risk devices only under conditions, so this safeguard is barely being used.

literature.citation: Gandjour, A. (2026), Evaluating the impact of the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR) on mortality and device availability in Germany, PLoS ONE 21(7):e0350175
literature.title: Evaluating the impact of the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR) on mortality and device availability in Germany
literature.method: simulation model (top-down life-table elasticity and bottom-up device-level) under explicit assumptions
literature.outcomes: device-related deaths avoided vs deaths from withdrawals and certification delays
literature.headline: Market withdrawals and certification delays were modelled to cause an estimated 163-1,884 additional deaths per year plus a one-time burden of 700-4,200 deaths. Under central assumptions the MDR is consistent with long-run reductions in device-related deaths (official German reports attribute about 17 deaths a year to devices; international estimates go up to 2,500).
literature.summary_plain: A modelling study suggests the MDR could save lives over time but may cost lives in the short run through device withdrawals and delays, especially for niche and paediatric devices.
